<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is blood that has been corrupted in that part where the wound is, and it is the effect of a corrupted digestion in that same place. To have corrupted the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the parts, and finally to have converted the blood into pus—this is exactly what is reputed in the **Schools** <note>the medical universities following traditional Galenic and Aristotelian doctrines</note> to have countered **Catarrhs** <gloss>down-flows of waste fluid</gloss>. They claim either that the excrementitious humor (which otherwise threatened to settle upon a **noble part** <gloss>a vital organ</gloss>) was extracted through the hole of the cautery from the head (from where they originally trace all **Catarrhs**), or that in the meantime there is a consensus between the head and the wounded part, or not; for it is all the same, provided the wounded skin is kept open. Whether that excrementitious humor is blood, or whether it becomes pus or **sanies** <gloss>thin, fetid discharge</gloss>, it is all the same, as long as the world is deceived by the worn-out terms of **Catarrh**, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and **fontanelle** <gloss>a small artificial ulcer or "little fountain" kept open for drainage</gloss>. For I observe a year-old infant, now teething, suffering from a fever, foaming at the mouth, and incessant saliva. And finally, there are griping pains in the bowels and stools of a greenish-yellow color. At the very least, that tooth is a part of the head; therefore, the diarrhea will be a **Catarrh** of the head. But what is the consensus of a tooth about to break through, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what power does it have to produce and send a **Catarrh** from the infant's stomach to the head, and from there into the **Ileum** <gloss>the third part of the small intestine</gloss>? By what right does the vapor distilled from the stomach become copper-green bile in the head? Has the workshop of the biles perhaps already migrated to the head from the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were able to tolerate it) drive away that leek-green diarrhea into itself? And could a few drops of pus compensate for several pounds of leek-green bile? Why does the infant’s stomach manufacture **Catarrh** because of the pain of a tooth? Why is it sent into the intestine and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a **Catarrh**? Rather, the indignant **Archeus** <gloss>the internal vital spirit or "chief worker" governing the body’s functions</gloss> is ready anywhere, especially in the intestine, to transform the alimentary cream into excrements, which are thought by the **Schools** to be bile, phlegm, and so on. If, therefore, diarrhea does not become a **Catarrh**, and if the **Archeus**, being indignant, is able

<column-break/>

to transform anything into a hostile liquor whenever the gum is afflicted, will he not be able to discharge himself in any direction through the established **emunctories** <gloss>natural excretory organs or passages</gloss>? Must he wait for the skin to be opened by a caustic? Ah, what cruel dullness has made the **Schools** act so ferociously against their fellow mortals?

<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not consider that in women and the obese, there is a fleshy membrane around the ordinary locations of the cautery—mere **axungia** <gloss>soft animal fat or lard</gloss> at least two fingers thick—yet cauteries are persuaded upon these persons more frequently and as more profitable. For this reason, the bottom of the **fontanelle** will hardly reach the middle of the fat. 

<margin>17.</margin>
There is, therefore, no path by which the fictitious evil humor proscribed as **Catarrh** can rush from the brain, or between the skull and the skin, through the middle of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor, which by its own sin is proscribed by the sending part, and descending unmixed through the substance of the fat, degenerates into pus? If it is an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why will it not be more frequent in younger and hot stomachs than in weak, old, and cold ones? In what way will that water, distilled from vapor, take on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the **meninges** <gloss>membranes covering the brain</gloss>, and the skull to find the hole made by the cautery, so that it may flow down and be purged by that way alone? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times sooner before it reaches the place assigned by the physician's pleasure for the cautery? How can water rising from the stomach already be blood and the mother of pus? How can blood (the matter of pus, according to **Galen**) be the matter of **Catarrh**? Why should blood be reduced to the series of evil humors, which, not yet contaminated, is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once a wound is made, will nature stop thrusting down the damned matter through and into the places accustomed to it? For will it, because the skin has been opened at the physician’s whim, become ignorant of its wandering paths? Did it perhaps labor so much only to find an exit somewhere? And now that one is made, will it henceforth come into obedience to the one who wounds? Therefore, these four things are false:

<summary>Van Helmont refutes the Galenic theory of catarrh by arguing that internal ailments, such as an infant's diarrhea during teething, are caused by the Archeus's reaction to pain rather than fluids draining from the brain. He further argues that artificial ulcers (fontanelles) cannot drain humors through thick layers of body fat as traditional medicine claims.</summary>
<keywords>cautery, catarrh, Archeus, fontanelle, teething, bile, medical theory, Galen, adipose tissue, anatomy</keywords>
